topics.title: Architecture
topics.short_abstract: How do buildings shape cognition? My work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms through which architectural features—ceiling height, natural light, spatial layout, material texture—affect how people think, feel, and behave. This research bridges cognitive science, neuroscience, and architectural design, asking how we can design buildings that actively support human wellbeing, creativity, and social interaction.
topics.long_summary:
Architecture is not a backdrop to human activity; it is a cognitive partner. My research program in cognitive neuroscience for architecture investigates how the built environment shapes perception, attention, stress, creativity, and social behavior through mechanisms grounded in predictive processing, allostatic regulation, and embodied cognition.

A central insight from this work is that architectural interactivity differs fundamentally from human-computer interaction. In buildings, there is no fixed digital-physical interface: people reconfigure chairs, adjust lighting, leave doors open, and continuously reshape the spatial ensemble that scaffolds social activity. This 'lightweight reconfigurability' means architectural space is appropriated and re-appropriated dozens of times a day—something that HCI systems can only weakly duplicate through customization.

I have developed a systematic framework—the Web of Belief for Architecture—that maps over 180 neuroscience-backed design templates connecting specific environmental features (e.g., fractal complexity, biophilic elements, daylight spectrum) to cognitive and emotional outcomes. Each template carries a calibrated confidence score and is grounded in primary research, forming a Quinean web of mutually supporting evidence that architects can use to make evidence-based design decisions.

This work draws on collaborations with the Academy of Neuroscience for Architecture (ANFA), the Bartlett School of Architecture at UCL (where I held a Leverhulme Fellowship), and ongoing partnerships with architectural firms seeking to integrate cognitive science into their design process.
key_findings: Architectural space is 'lightweight reconfigurable'—people reshape spatial ensembles dozens of times daily, unlike fixed digital interfaces
Buildings create 'intimacy gradients' through ceiling height, room size, and natural light that shape our sense of privacy, seclusion, and social openness
The Web of Belief framework maps 180+ design templates from neuroscience findings to specific architectural features with calibrated confidence scores
Architects think about interactivity as a 3D spatial ensemble rather than a state-space of forced choices
Environmental features affect perception through embodied mechanisms—tools, spaces, and bodily states change what we see and how we act

topics.title: Choreography
topics.short_abstract: Dance is thinking with the body. My research with world-class choreographers—particularly a decade-long collaboration with Wayne McGregor and Random Dance—reveals how expert movers use their bodies as cognitive instruments: marking movements to reduce complexity, distributing memory across dancers, and using physical exploration to generate ideas that could never arise from purely mental deliberation.
topics.long_summary:
My research on choreography began with a simple observation: when dancers prepare for performance, they often 'mark' their movements—performing reduced, simplified versions of full phrases. Why? The conventional assumption was that marking is mere energy conservation. Through years of studying professional dancers at Wayne McGregor's Random Dance company, I discovered something far more interesting: marking is a form of thinking. It is an epistemic action that allows dancers to mentally simulate the full movement while their body provides just enough kinesthetic scaffolding to keep the thought process anchored.

This finding connects to a much broader theory about how bodily action supports cognition. When choreographers create new work, they are engaged in a deeply interactive process: they task dancers with movement problems, watch the physical solutions that emerge, and then select, modify, and recombine what they see. The choreographer's creative cognition is distributed across the bodies of multiple dancers, the spatial layout of the studio, and the music or sonic environment. Memory for dance sequences is similarly distributed—no single dancer holds the entire piece in mind; the group collectively remembers through social coordination and spatial cuing.

I have also studied how dancers use the space around them as an external memory and planning resource, including how spatial landmarks in the studio anchor movement sequences, and how the 'feel' of a movement phrase serves as a retrieval cue for what comes next. This work has been presented at venues ranging from the Wellcome Foundation and the Victoria & Albert Museum to the Guggenheim and multiple international dance science conferences.
key_findings: Marking in dance is an epistemic action—a way of thinking with the body, not just conserving energy
Choreographic creativity is distributed across multiple dancers' bodies, spatial layout, and sonic environment
Memory for dance is socially distributed—no single dancer holds the entire piece; the group remembers collectively
Physical exploration generates movement ideas that could never arise from purely mental deliberation
Spatial landmarks in the studio serve as external memory anchors for movement sequences

topics.title: Creativity
topics.short_abstract: Creativity is not a purely internal flash of insight—it is deeply interactive. My research shows that creative cognition depends on working with external things: sketches, prototypes, instruments, other people. By interacting with materials and ideas in their environment, creative thinkers recruit resources that broaden and deepen their thinking in ways that purely mental deliberation cannot match.
topics.long_summary:
The traditional psychological study of creativity focused on insight problems—moments when a person suddenly breaks through a cognitive set to see a solution they were previously blind to. My research extends this tradition by showing that insight is not just an internal event: it arises from interaction with the physical and social environment.

A central concept in my work is 'deep processing through interaction.' Deep processing was traditionally understood as an internal affair—recruiting more semantic associations, beliefs, and ideas. I argue that deep processing is better understood as working with things in a tightly coupled way so as to deepen thinking. Writing about a topic, sketching a design, or discussing an idea with a colleague are all forms of interactive deep processing that bring more resources online—both internal (neural activation) and external (representations, prototypes, other people's perspectives).

This applies across domains. Architects deep-process by making sketches and 3D models, then reflecting on them from different angles. Mathematicians work with symbols and diagrams, building intermediate constructions that serve as persistent reminders and stepping stones. Choreographers experiment with movement phrases; musicians play with sound. In each case, externalizing thought and working with the material products of that externalization is integral to the creative process.

My experimental work, including studies with Viasat and at Trinity Laban Conservatoire, has demonstrated that chance encounters with environmental side-effects significantly increase creative problem-solving—just as Duncker showed that accidentally seeing the tack box empty dramatically helps subjects solve the candle problem. Interactivity and chance are partners in creativity.
key_findings: Creative cognition depends on interaction with external materials—sketches, prototypes, instruments, other people
Deep processing is better understood as interactive coupling with external resources than as purely internal activation
Chance encounters with environmental side-effects significantly increase creative insight
Architects, mathematicians, dancers, and musicians all create through cyclical externalization-reflection loops
The longer and more varied the interaction with materials, the broader the set of resources recruited for creative thinking

topics.title: Embodied, Extended, Situated
topics.short_abstract: What does it mean to think with your body—and with the things around you? My work on the 4E's (Embodied, Embedded, Extended, Enactive cognition) explores how tools, environments, and bodily states reshape perception, expand our cognitive capacities, and blur the boundary between mind and world. When we wield a tool, our brain literally incorporates it into our body schema, changing what we perceive and how we act.
topics.long_summary:
The 4E approach to cognition—Embodied, Embedded, Extended, and Enactive—represents a fundamental rethinking of what it means to have a mind. My research has contributed to each of these strands, with a particular focus on how tools and environmental structures extend cognitive capacities beyond the biological brain.

A key finding from my work on embodied cognition is that tools change perception. When a tool is incorporated into our body schema, our perception of space, distance, and affordances changes. Hills look steeper with a heavy backpack; warehouse aisles seem shorter on roller skates; a carpenter with a chisel sees locations where it can be applied. This is not metaphorical—it reflects genuine changes in how the brain represents the body and its capacities.

The 'extended mind' thesis, which I have both defended and refined, asks: when does a cognitive process genuinely extend beyond the skull? My answer focuses on the quality of coupling between a person and their external resources. Tight coupling—where the external resource is reliably available, readily accessible, and functionally integrated into the person's cognitive workflow—can create genuinely extended cognitive systems. A mathematician's notebook, a chef's mise en place, or a dancer's marked score are not mere memory aids; they are constitutive parts of the thinking process.

I have also explored the limits of embodied extension: how different can a prosthetic body part be before we cannot assimilate it? Research on remapping virtual hands (Iriki's work with monkeys) suggests that anatomical mappings are surprisingly flexible—but there are limits that we are only beginning to understand. These questions are directly relevant to VR, XR, and the design of prosthetic and robotic systems.
key_findings: Tools change perception—a chisel in hand lets you 'see' where cement should go; a heavy backpack makes hills look steeper
Our body schema can incorporate tools, vehicles, and even virtual body parts, changing what we perceive as reachable space
Genuine cognitive extension requires tight coupling: reliable availability, easy access, and functional integration with internal processes
Skill with a tool partly determines which affordances are visible—experts detect more tool-relevant features than novices
Goals and attention hyperbolically warp perceived space—we exaggerate what we care about and compress what we don't

topics.title: Interactivity
topics.short_abstract: Interactivity is the engine of thought. My theory of interactivity explains how people amplify their cognitive powers by physically manipulating their environment—rearranging Scrabble tiles, gesturing while speaking, sketching while designing. These are not idle fidgets; they are epistemic actions that make thinking faster, more reliable, and more creative than pure mental deliberation alone.
topics.long_summary:
My theory of interactivity is built on a fundamental distinction between two kinds of action: pragmatic actions (actions that move the world closer to a physical goal) and epistemic actions (actions that change the world to make mental computation easier, faster, or more reliable). When a Scrabble player rearranges tiles on their rack, they are not moving closer to placing a word on the board—they are making it easier to see which words are possible. This is an epistemic action.

Epistemic actions are everywhere. We point to keep our place while counting, rotate objects instead of mentally rotating them, lay out ingredients before cooking (mise en place), write down intermediate results while computing, and gesture while explaining ideas. In each case, the person is using the physical world as an external cognitive resource—offloading memory, reducing the complexity of mental computation, or creating new representations that make patterns visible.

I am currently writing a book on interactivity that develops this theory into a comprehensive framework explaining why interactive cognition is more powerful than detached, purely mental cognition. The framework addresses several key questions: What makes some interactions 'cognitively profitable'? How do people learn to use their environment as a thinking tool? Why is physical manipulation often more effective than visualization for certain kinds of problem-solving? And how should we design interfaces—both digital and architectural—to support interactive cognition?

This work has been recognized with an ACM Notable Publication award for 'Embodied Cognition and the Magical Future of Interaction Design' (2013), and has influenced thinking in HCI, architecture, dance science, and educational design.
key_findings: Epistemic actions—actions that change the world to simplify thought—are as fundamental to cognition as pragmatic actions
Rearranging Scrabble tiles, gesturing while talking, and mise en place in cooking are all forms of interactive cognition
Interactive cognition is more powerful than detached mental deliberation because it offloads memory, reduces computational complexity, and creates new representations
ACM Notable Publication 2013 for 'Embodied Cognition and the Magical Future of Interaction Design'
The theory of interactivity has practical implications for HCI, architecture, dance, and educational design

topics.title: Planning
topics.short_abstract: How do people plan in complex, dynamic environments? My early work at MIT's AI Lab investigated how intelligent agents plan actions in real-time when the world changes unpredictably. This research bridged artificial intelligence and cognitive science, showing that effective planning requires continuous interaction with the environment rather than complete mental simulation before acting.
topics.long_summary:
My work on planning began at MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, where I studied how intelligent agents—both human and artificial—can plan effectively in dynamic, unpredictable environments. The classical AI approach assumed that planning was a purely computational process: construct a complete plan mentally, then execute it. My research showed that this approach fails in real-world situations where the environment is too complex, too dynamic, or too uncertain to model completely in advance.

Instead, effective planners interleave planning and execution. They take actions that reveal information about the world, use the results to revise their plans, and exploit environmental structure to simplify the planning problem. This 'situated planning' perspective anticipates much of my later work on epistemic actions and interactive cognition: the idea that intelligent behavior does not emerge from detached computation but from tight coupling between an agent and its environment.

This early work laid the groundwork for understanding why people naturally use their physical surroundings as planning aids—why we lay things out, make lists, use timelines, and create physical arrangements that externalize our goals and progress. It also connects to my later interests in how architects and designers plan—using sketches, models, and prototypes rather than purely mental visualizations.
key_findings: Effective planning requires interleaving planning and execution rather than complete mental simulation
Actions that reveal environmental information (exploratory actions) are as important as goal-directed actions
Environmental structure can simplify the planning problem—people exploit spatial layout to reduce search
Anticipates the theory of epistemic actions: intelligence emerges from agent-environment coupling
Grounds later work on how architects use sketches and models as externalized planning tools

topics.title: Representation
topics.short_abstract: How do external representations—diagrams, notations, maps, models—shape thought? My research investigates why some representations make problems easy and others make them hard, and how the choice of representational format affects what people can see, infer, and discover. This work connects cognitive science to practical questions about information design, data visualization, and architectural drawing.
topics.long_summary:
A core insight from cognitive science is that the way information is represented profoundly affects how easily it can be used. My research on representation explores this insight across multiple domains: mathematical notation, architectural drawing, data visualization, and everyday diagrams.

One line of work examines how different external representations of the same problem can make it trivially easy or extremely difficult. For instance, the same logical problem can be expressed in sentential (linguistic) form or diagrammatic form, with dramatically different effects on how quickly and accurately people solve it. Diagrams support certain inferences by making spatial relationships directly visible, while sentential representations require chains of deduction. Understanding these trade-offs is essential for designing effective notations, dashboards, and visual interfaces.

I have also studied how people actively construct and modify representations as part of their problem-solving process—creating sketches, annotating diagrams, and reorganizing visual displays to highlight patterns. This representational tinkering is itself a form of epistemic action: by changing the external representation, people change what they can see and think. This connects my work on representation to my broader theory of interactivity.

Practical applications include guidelines for information architects and data visualization designers about how to choose representational formats that best support the cognitive tasks their users face.
key_findings: The format of a representation profoundly affects problem-solving speed, accuracy, and the insights people can reach
Diagrams support different inferences than sentential representations—making spatial relationships directly visible
People actively modify external representations as a problem-solving strategy (representational tinkering)
Representational choice is an epistemic action—changing the display changes what you can think
Has practical implications for information architecture, data visualization, and notation design

topics.title: Perceptual Thinking
topics.short_abstract: Can you think with your eyes? My research on perceptual thinking investigates how visual and spatial reasoning go beyond passive seeing. When experts look at a chess board, an architectural plan, or a mathematical diagram, they are not just registering what's there—they are actively projecting, imagining, and reasoning through what they see. Perception itself is a form of cognition.
topics.long_summary:
Perceptual thinking is the idea that perception is not just a passive input channel but an active cognitive process. When an experienced chess player looks at a board position, they don't just see pieces—they see threats, opportunities, and developing combinations. When an architect looks at a building plan, they see potential movements through space, light conditions at different times of day, and social interactions the layout will afford.

My research explores how this 'thinking through seeing' works. A key concept is projection: the ability to mentally overlay imagined elements onto a perceived scene. When a designer imagines how a wall would look if moved three feet to the right, they are projecting an alternative reality onto their current perception. This projection ability is central to design cognition—it allows people to evaluate possibilities without physically realizing them.

I distinguish between physical thinking (reasoning about how physical objects behave) and visual thinking (reasoning by manipulating visual images). Both are forms of perceptual cognition, but they draw on different neural resources. Physical thinking engages our embodied intuitions about forces, balance, and material properties. Visual thinking engages our capacity for mental imagery and spatial transformation.

This research has implications for how we design visualization tools, architectural drawing systems, and educational materials—all of which should support the natural projective and imaginative capacities of their users.
key_findings: Perception is an active cognitive process—experts see possibilities, threats, and affordances, not just objects
Projection allows people to mentally overlay imagined alternatives onto perceived scenes
Physical thinking (about forces, balance, materials) and visual thinking (spatial transformation) engage different neural resources
Design cognition fundamentally depends on the ability to project alternatives onto current perceptions
Has implications for visualization tools, architectural drawing, and educational design

topics.title: Implicit/Explicit
topics.short_abstract: Much of what we know, we know without knowing that we know it. My research on implicit and explicit cognition explores the boundary between conscious, deliberate thought and the vast unconscious processes that shape our behavior. How much of skilled performance is explicitly planned versus implicitly guided? When can implicit knowledge be made explicit—and does doing so help or hinder performance?
topics.long_summary:
The distinction between implicit and explicit cognition runs through all of my research areas. In dance, a choreographer may explicitly tell a dancer to 'reach higher,' but the dancer's ability to execute the movement gracefully depends on implicit motor knowledge that cannot be fully verbalized. In architecture, designers may explicitly state their design intent (e.g., 'create a welcoming entrance'), but their implicit knowledge of materials, proportions, and human behavior shapes their solutions in ways they cannot fully articulate.

My research investigates several questions at this boundary: When does making implicit knowledge explicit improve performance? (Sometimes it helps, as when a teacher explains a technique. But sometimes it hurts, as when a skilled performer 'overthinks' a movement.) How do people develop implicit expertise through interaction with their environment? And how do we design environments and tools that support both modes of cognition?

This work connects to my interests in architecture (buildings affect us through implicit channels—we don't consciously register ceiling height but it affects our cognitive style), creativity (many creative breakthroughs involve the sudden explicit recognition of something that was implicitly known), and interactivity (epistemic actions often operate by making implicit possibilities explicit—e.g., rearranging tiles makes hidden words visible).
key_findings: Skilled performance depends on implicit motor and perceptual knowledge that cannot be fully verbalized
Making implicit knowledge explicit sometimes helps (teaching) and sometimes hurts (overthinking)
Buildings affect cognition through implicit channels—ceiling height, light, materials operate below conscious awareness
Creative breakthroughs often involve sudden explicit recognition of implicitly known patterns
Epistemic actions work partly by making implicit possibilities explicit—rearranging things reveals hidden structure
